explain.say: In 1802 the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India began measuring the subcontinent with theodolites, one of them weighing about half a tonne. Decades later its angles revealed the height of Mount Everest. Your theodolite is much lighter but does the same job: it measures angles. Here are its working parts.

explain.say: Here is a modern survey instrument in 3D, the total station: a theodolite with a laser rangefinder built in. Look at the telescope, the tribrach and the levelling screws on the tripod. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

explain.say: First set it up right over the station, using the plumb, then turn the levelling screws until the bubble sits centred. Now sight point A and read the horizontal circle: eighty five degrees, twenty five minutes. Swing to point C: one hundred and thirty two degrees, forty five minutes, twenty seconds. The difference is the angle.

explain.say: Small errors in the instrument creep in, so surveyors flip the telescope over and turn it round, then measure again. That is face left and face right. Face left gives forty seven degrees twenty minutes ten seconds, face right thirty seconds. The average, twenty seconds, cancels the error. Why does averaging help?

explain.say: Because the error flips sign between faces! Now the vertical circle. Stand fifty metres from a tower and tilt up to its top: twelve degrees. The height above your eye is fifty times the tangent of twelve degrees, ten point six three metres. Add the instrument height of one point five, and the tower is about twelve point one metres tall.

explain.say: Modern digital theodolites read to one second of arc, about half a millimetre sideways at a hundred metres. Superb work! Exam tip: draw a sketch with the angle and the distance before you calculate. Challenge: at thirty metres, the top of a mast is at twenty degrees and the instrument is one point five metres high. faq.a: A precise instrument for measuring horizontal and vertical angles. A telescope turns on a vertical axis over a horizontal circle and on a horizontal axis against a vertical circle.

faq.q: How do you measure a horizontal angle with a theodolite?
faq.a: Centre and level the instrument over the station, sight the first point and read the horizontal circle, then turn to the second point and read again. The difference is the angle.

faq.q: Why take face left and face right readings?
faq.a: Reading on both faces and averaging cancels instrument errors such as collimation and trunnion axis errors, because they have opposite signs on the two faces.

faq.q: How do you find the height of a building with a theodolite?
faq.a: Measure the horizontal distance and the vertical angle to the top. The height above the instrument is distance times the tangent of the angle; add the instrument height.

faq.a: Survey theodolites read to between 1 and 20 seconds of arc. One second is about half a millimetre at 100 metres.
